one_liner: Research Lua 5.1 VM whose interpreter is generated by Deegen; about 1.3x LuaJIT's interpreter and 2.8x PUC Lua 5.1.
what_it_does: LuaJIT Remake (LJR) is a Lua 5.1 implementation built as the case study for Deegen, a meta-compiler that turns bytecode semantics written as C++ functions (annotated/bytecodes) into an interpreter, a copy-and-patch baseline JIT and the tier-switching logic between them. It ships one standalone executable, `luajitr <script> [args]`, with no options, no REPL and no documented embedding or Lua C API. The parser comes from LuaJIT (lj_lex.cpp, lj_parse.cpp) and the runtime is new: tables use hidden classes instead of hash tables.
how_it_is_fast: Each bytecode handler is compiled through LLVM IR as a function using LLVM's GHC calling convention, which has no callee-saved registers and is patched here to pass more arguments. Handlers end in guaranteed tail calls, so dispatch is continuation passing with the VM state pinned in registers. Deegen also generates inline caches for table and call sites, type-speculation fast paths, and slow paths split out of the hot code (deegen_ast_inline_cache, deegen_call_inline_cache, deegen_ast_slow_path). Tables use hidden-class 'structures' with butterfly storage (runtime/structure.h, butterfly.h), so property access can be served from an inline cache.
when_to_use: Research or teaching on interpreter and JIT construction: seeing how a generated interpreter (Deegen) can beat LuaJIT's hand-written assembler interpreter.
Benchmark studies of dispatch techniques (GHC-convention tail calls, inline caching, hidden classes) on x86-64 Linux, using the 44 scripts in luabench/.
Running self-contained, short-lived Lua 5.1 batch scripts on x86-64 Linux where memory growth without GC is acceptable and the scripts do not need require/module.
when_not_to_use: Anything long-running or allocation-heavy: there is no garbage collector, so memory only grows.
Embedding in a C/C++ application: only the standalone luajitr binary exists; there is no documented Lua C API, FFI or REPL, and the package library (require, module) is missing.
Platforms other than x86-64 Linux, or CPUs without BMI, SSE4 and FSGSBASE (the release build uses -mbmi -msse4 -mfsgsbase).
Peak throughput: per the paper abstract, LJR's baseline JIT is on average 33% slower than LuaJIT's optimizing tracing JIT (faster on 13 of 44 benchmarks), and the optimizing (DFG) tier is unfinished.
Production use: the README calls it a work in progress far from production-ready, and the last commit is 2025-02-18.

integration.form: standalone executable (luajitr); no library or embedding API documented
integration.dependencies: Build: Docker plus python3; the build runs inside the haoranxu510/ljr-build:v0.0.7 image (Ubuntu 20.04 with Clang+LLVM 19.1.6 built from source with three local patches). Runtime dependencies: not documented.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; patched Clang/LLVM 19.1.6 from the project's Docker image (stock compilers are not supported because the code uses the patched GHC and PreserveMost calling conventions)
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux only (CPU with BMI, SSE4 and FSGSBASE)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: runs Lua 5.1 scripts as `luajitr script.lua` like `lua script.lua`, but it has no options, no REPL, no C API, no require/module and no GC, so it cannot replace PUC Lua 5.1 or LuaJIT in an application

gotchas: Harness and reproduction flaw: the README's 34.6% / 185% numbers were last updated 2022-11-26, when only the interpreter existed. At HEAD, deegen/deegen_options.h sets x_allow_interpreter_tier_up_to_baseline_jit = true and VM::Create defaults to EngineMaxTier::Unrestricted, and standalone/main.cpp exposes no switch. A HEAD build of luajitr therefore moves each function to the baseline JIT after it has executed 20x its bytecode length, so `bash run_bench.sh` measures interpreter plus baseline JIT rather than the interpreter the README compares. To reproduce the claim you must edit that constant or build a 2022 commit.

run_bench.sh times only luajitr; the PUC Lua 5.1 and LuaJIT baselines are not scripted, and how their GC was disabled is not documented. It sends stdout and stderr to /dev/null and checks only the exit code, so output correctness is not verified. bench_pretty_format.py reports the mean of the middle 5 of 7 runs (fastest and slowest dropped), while the README footnote says 5 repetitions.

There are three different headline figures: the 2022-11-22 blog says 28% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter and 171% faster than PUC Lua; the README says 34.6% and 185%; the peer-reviewed paper abstract (search snippet only) says 31% and 179% over 44 benchmarks. Cite the paper's figure.
GC was turned off in every implementation, so the comparison leaves out collector cost entirely, and a real LJR deployment would run out of memory where PUC Lua or LuaJIT would not.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For production embedding, pick a maintained sibling such as Luau (which also beats PUC Lua 5.x with its interpreter) or Daslang, because LJR has no GC, no C API and no commits since 2025-02-18; pick yklua for a JIT on current PUC Lua 5.5 semantics. Pick LJR only to study or reuse the Deegen approach, or to compare interpreter designs on Lua 5.1 code.
verified_claims_summary: Across 44 Lua benchmarks on an Intel i7-12700H laptop, pinned to one core, with GC off in all VMs, LJR's generated interpreter ran about 1.31x faster than LuaJIT 2.1's interpreter (JIT off) and 2.79x faster than PUC Lua 5.1 by geometric mean (paper abstract via search snippet; the 2022 README says 1.346x and 2.85x). Baseline versions and build flags are not given in the repo, and the bench script times only luajitr, which now tiers up to the baseline JIT by default.
status_note: Stale research code (last commit 2025-02-18, mid-way through an unfinished DFG optimizing tier), Apache-2.0, buildable only through the author's Docker image with a patched LLVM; usable for study but not for shipping.
